b: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) gets its own profile in The New Yorker today.

The profile‘s author, Sheon Han, writes about how he “laughed in disbelief” when, years ago as an undergraduate, he learned of the SEP. Unfortunately, it was after he had just submitted a paper for a class. Reading its entry on the topic of his paper, he says, was eye-opening:

After reading the entry, which ran to more than ten thousand words, I felt at once elated and rebuked: I’d just been exposed to perhaps the finest distillation of what humanity had to say about the topic, but it was also clear that my paper didn’t contain an iota of original insight.
The profile relays some of the history of the SEP and the context of its beginnings:

The S.E.P. began [in 1995] with two text files on Zalta’s computer, about Turing machines and the German philosopher Gottlob Frege. Despite these modest beginnings, its telos was clear: to become a peer-reviewed reference work that would reflect advancements in the field, an objective that its more physical counterparts had failed to achieve. The most comprehensive philosophy encyclopedia at the time, the Macmillan Encyclopedia, from 1967, had yet to include major developments from luminaries such as Saul Kripke, Hilary Putnam, and John Rawls.
The article also discusses the SEP’s professional significance and a bit about its editorial processes.
And while we’re on the subject, don’t forget about this browser plug-in for the SEP which improves the user experience in several ways.
